item.research_question: How does helium ion implantation affect the mechanical behavior of nanocrystalline tungsten, specifically regarding the competition between softening mechanisms and hardening mechanisms across different temperatures and fluences?
item.material_system: Nanocrystalline tungsten containing a distribution of elongated nanocrystalline and ultrafine grains
item.processing_route: Orthogonal machining followed by polishing; Helium ion implantation ex situ at 30 °C and 500 °C (4 keV He+, flux 5.45 × 10^18 He·m−2·s−1, fluence up to 1.0 × 10^22 He·m−2) and in situ at 30, 500, and 950 °C (4 keV or 2 keV He+, flux 3.2 × 10^16 He·m−2·s−1, fluences 2.0 × 10^19–3.2 × 10^20 He·m−2)
item.test_conditions: Nanoindentation at room temperature using a diamond Berkovich probe (radius 50 nm), constant indentation strain rate of 0.5 s−1, maximum load of 3 mN, contact depth <85 nm
key_findings: Pristine nanocrystalline tungsten exhibited a hardness of 8.7 ± 0.3 GPa and reduced modulus of 302 ± 30.0 GPa.
Room temperature implantation to a fluence of 3.6 × 10^19 He·m−2 produced a significant reduction in hardness and modulus relative to the pristine sample.
An order of magnitude increase in fluence to 3.2 × 10^20 He·m−2 was accompanied by an increase in both hardness and modulus compared to the lower fluence condition.
At a fluence of 1.0 × 10^22 He·m−2, the hardness exceeded the pristine nanocrystalline tungsten sample, resembling classical irradiation hardening.
Implantation at 950 °C to a fluence of 3.2 × 10^20 He·m−2 resulted in faceted cavities in grain boundaries with an average size of 7.5 ± 1.3 nm.
Intragranular defect loop damage emerged with the increase in fluence to 3.2 × 10^20 He·m−2 at 950 °C, which was absent at the lower fluence.
Samples implanted at temperatures up to 500 °C showed a linear scaling of hardness and modulus with fluence, whereas samples at 950 °C deviated from this trend.
item.mechanism: Softening is attributed to bubble/cavity loaded grain boundaries suppressing the activation barrier for the onset of plasticity via grain boundary mediated dislocation nucleation, while hardening at higher fluences is caused by intragranular defect loops inhibiting dislocation slip.
item.limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.
item.future_work: The authors propose further exploration of competing mechanisms in nanocrystalline metals with particular focus on implantation conditions that produce cavity loaded grain boundaries collectively with intragranular defect damage.
quotes: Softening was apparent across all implantation temperatures and attributed to bubble/cavity loaded grain boundaries suppressing the activation barrier for the onset of plasticity via grain boundary mediated dislocation nucleation.
Hardening from intragranular defect loop damage thus competes with bubble/cavity induced grain boundary softening and the mechanisms underpinning this transition are discussed.
Voids are known to act as stress concentrations that reduce the energetic barrier for dislocation nucleation from grain boundaries as well as accelerate grain boundary mediated deformation processes.
